lead: Today the Syro-Malabar Church remembers the coming of St Thomas the Apostle to India, and the whole Church keeps the Presentation of the Blessed Virgin Mary. The readings are chosen for the apostle. In Exodus, God calls Moses, a man who doubts his own words, and sends him with a promise of redemption. In Isaiah, God tells the servant he called “from the ends of the earth”: “Do not fear, I will help you.” In Ephesians, the Gentiles, once far off, become a holy temple “built upon the foundation of the apostles”. In John, it is Thomas who asks the question that draws from Jesus the words “I am the way, and the truth, and the life”. The line runs from a reluctant messenger to an apostle who carried the way to a distant land, and its key words are sending, foundation and way.

The Presentation of Mary fits the same readings. A holy temple, a dwelling place for God (Ephesians 2:21–22), was first prepared in her, the young girl wholly given to God, who would become the dwelling place of the Word.

set: Moses' first visit to Pharaoh has failed. Pharaoh has made the slaves' work harder, and the Israelite foremen blame Moses (Exodus 5). Moses complains to God: “Why did you ever send me?” (5:22). In chapter 6 God answers by renewing his promise and his name: “I am the Lord” (6:2). Many scholars see in 6:2–13 a second account of Moses' call, parallel to the burning bush in chapter 3, from another strand of Israel's tradition.
str: vv. 6–8: God's promise, framed by “I am the Lord”: a series of “I will” sentences.
v. 9: the people cannot listen, crushed by slavery.
vv. 10–11: God sends Moses again to Pharaoh.
v. 12: Moses objects: “how then shall Pharaoh listen to me, poor speaker that I am?”
v. 13: God gives Moses and Aaron their charge.
kw: The verb of the gō’ēl, the next of kin whose duty was to buy back a relative sold into slavery or to rescue his land (Leviticus 25:25, 47–49). God acts as Israel's next of kin. The same word returns in today's second reading: “your Redeemer” (Isaiah 41:14).
Literally “shortness of spirit” or “shortness of breath”. Oppression had taken away the people's very breath, so that they could not hear good news.
Literally “uncircumcised of lips”: lips that seem closed, unfit for God's message. Moses feels unworthy, but God's call does not depend on the messenger's eloquence.
vv: I will redeem you with an outstretched arm and with mighty acts of judgment.
Jewish tradition counts four promises of redemption in vv. 6–7 (bring out, deliver, redeem, take), and links them with the four cups of wine at the Passover meal.
I will take you as my people, and I will be your God.
The covenant formula, repeated through the whole Bible until its last book: “they will be his peoples, and God himself will be with them” (Revelation 21:3).
The Israelites have not listened to me; how then shall Pharaoh listen to me, poor speaker that I am?
Every apostle knows this fear. God's answer is not to remove the difficulty but to repeat the command. The mission rests on God's word, not on the messenger's talent.
ch: The Catechism presents Moses' call as a model of prayer: God calls, Moses hesitates and objects, and in the end he learns to cooperate with God's plan (CCC 2575). The Church reads the Exodus as the great figure of Christ's redemption, celebrated in every Holy Qurbana as our Passover (CCC 1363–1364). On this feast, Moses sent to Pharaoh reminds us of an apostle sent across the sea to a people he did not know.

r.h: Do not fear, I will help you
set: This oracle belongs to the Book of Consolation (Isaiah 40–55), addressed to the exiles in Babylon. The nations tremble before the rise of Cyrus (41:1–7) and make new idols for protection. To Israel, small and weak, God speaks words of tenderness. This is the first passage in Isaiah to call Israel “my servant”, a title that will grow into the figure of the Suffering Servant (52:13–53:12).
str: vv. 8–9: Israel, servant, chosen, offspring of Abraham, called from the ends of the earth.
v. 10: “do not fear, for I am with you”.
vv. 11–13: Israel's enemies shall come to nothing; God holds Israel's right hand.
vv. 14–16: “you worm Jacob”: the weak will become a threshing sledge, and will rejoice in the Holy One of Israel.
kw: Literally “the one who loves me” or “my beloved”. Abraham is called God's friend also in 2 Chronicles 20:7 and James 2:23. Islam too knows Abraham as the friend of God.
Repeated three times. In the Bible this word comes before great calls: to Abraham (Genesis 15:1), to Mary (Luke 1:30), to the women at the tomb (Matthew 28:10).
The same word as in Exodus 6:6. The Holy One of Israel is also Israel's next of kin, who takes responsibility for his poor relative.
vv: you whom I took from the ends of the earth, and called from its farthest corners, saying to you, “You are my servant, I have chosen you and not cast you off”;
do not fear, for I am with you, do not be afraid, for I am your God;
The reason for courage is not one's own strength but God's presence: “I am with you”. Jesus gives the same promise when he sends the apostles to all nations (Matthew 28:20).
Do not fear, you worm Jacob, you insect Israel! I will help you, says the Lord; your Redeemer is the Holy One of Israel.
The image is humbling but tender: God chooses what is small and makes it strong. The worm becomes a threshing sledge (v. 15).
ch: In the Magnificat Mary sings that God “has helped his servant Israel” (Luke 1:54), echoing this passage. The Church sees Isaiah's servant fulfilled in Christ, and the promise “I am with you” lived by the apostles. St Thomas, sent according to tradition to the farthest corners of the known world, carried this word to India: the God of Israel is the God of all nations (CCC 543, 849).

r.h: Built upon the foundation of the apostles
set: Ephesians was written to Christians most of whom were Gentiles, once “far off” from the covenants of Israel (2:12–13). In the Temple of Jerusalem a stone balustrade separated the Court of the Gentiles from the inner courts. Inscriptions on it, two of which have been found by archaeologists, warned that any foreigner who passed it would be responsible for his own death. Paul (or his disciple writing in his name) sees Christ's cross as breaking down every such wall of hostility.
str: vv. 14–16: Christ is our peace: he has made the two one, abolished the hostility, reconciled both to God through the cross.
vv. 17–18: he proclaimed peace to far and near; through him both have access in one Spirit to the Father.
vv. 19–22: no longer strangers: citizens, household, building, holy temple, dwelling place of God.
kw: The wall in the middle. The image recalls the Temple barrier, but the deeper wall is hostility between peoples and between humanity and God.
Resident foreigners without full rights. In Christ the Gentiles are no longer guests in God's house but members of the family.
From Isaiah 28:16 in the Greek Bible. The stone that holds the building together and sets its lines. The apostles are the foundation; Christ is the cornerstone.
vv: has broken down the dividing wall, that is, the hostility between us.
So then you are no longer strangers and aliens, but you are citizens with the saints and also members of the household of God,
The Gospel reached India as a homecoming, not as an import: the people of this land became members of God's household.
built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus himself as the cornerstone.
The “prophets” here are probably the prophets of the early Church, named with the apostles (compare 3:5; 4:11). The Church rests on the apostolic witness.
in whom you also are built together spiritually into a dwelling place for God.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the Church is apostolic because she is built on the foundation of the apostles, keeps their teaching and is guided by their successors (CCC 857, citing Ephesians 2:20). It also uses this passage for the image of the Church as God's building, with Christ as the cornerstone (CCC 756). The same image matches the season of Qudash Edtha, and today's Marian feast: Mary was the first and purest dwelling place of God among us.

r.h: Lord, how can we know the way?
set: Jesus speaks at the Last Supper, after washing the disciples' feet and foretelling Peter's denial (John 13). The disciples are troubled: he is going away. In this conversation three disciples interrupt with questions: Thomas (v. 5), Philip (v. 8), and later Judas, not Iscariot (v. 22). Thomas appears in John as a man of loyal courage (“Let us also go, that we may die with him”, 11:16), of honest questions (14:5) and, after Easter, of the highest confession of faith: “My Lord and my God!” (20:28).
str: vv. 1–4: “Do not let your hearts be troubled”; many dwelling places; I go to prepare a place; you know the way.
vv. 5–7: Thomas' question; “I am the way, and the truth, and the life”.
vv. 8–11: Philip's request; “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father”.
vv. 12–14: the believer will do greater works; whatever you ask in my name.
kw: From the verb menō, “to remain, abide”. Not temporary rooms but lasting homes with the Father. The same root gives the word for abiding in Christ (15:4).
The early Christians called their faith “the Way” (Acts 9:2). Jesus does not only show the way; he is the way.
To ask in Jesus' name is to pray as one united with him, according to his will, as his members.
vv: Do not let your hearts be troubled. Believe in God, believe also in me.
The same verb was used of Jesus himself, troubled at the tomb of Lazarus, in the hour of the cross and at the betrayal (11:33; 12:27; 13:21). He knows our trouble from within.
Lord, we do not know where you are going. How can we know the way?
Thomas does not pretend to understand. His honest question becomes a gift to the whole Church, because it draws out the answer of v. 6.
I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me.
St Augustine explains: as God, Christ is the homeland where we are going; as man, he is the way by which we go (in substance).
Whoever has seen me has seen the Father.
the one who believes in me will also do the works that I do and, in fact, will do greater works than these, because I am going to the Father.
“Greater” not in power but in reach: through the apostles, the Gospel would go beyond Galilee and Judea to the ends of the earth, to Rome and to India.
ch: The Catechism calls Jesus Christ, “the way, and the truth, and the life”, the first and last point of reference of all catechesis (CCC 1698), and teaches that his whole life reveals the Father: “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (CCC 516). Praying “in his name” is the newness of Christian prayer (CCC 2614). Pope Benedict XVI, in his catechesis on St Thomas (2006), said that Thomas' question gives us too the right to ask Jesus for explanations, and that Jesus' answer is meant for every seeker (in substance).

qa: Did St Thomas really come to India?

The Thomas Christians of Kerala have handed down from ancient times that the apostle landed at Kodungallur (Muziris), traditionally in AD 52, founded communities and died a martyr at Mylapore. Early writings from Syria, such as the third-century Acts of Thomas (a work with legendary elements) and the hymns of St Ephrem, link Thomas with India. Sea trade between the Roman world and the Malabar coast in the first century is well documented, so the journey was possible. The Church honours this living tradition, while historians weigh its details.
Is the Presentation of Mary in the Bible?

No. The story of the child Mary brought to the Temple comes from an early Christian writing, the Protoevangelium of James (second century), which is not part of Scripture. The feast is very old in the East and was linked with the dedication of the church of St Mary in Jerusalem in 543. Its truth is spiritual: Mary was wholly given to God from the beginning of her life (Marialis Cultus 8).
If Jesus is the only way, what about people of other religions?

The Church teaches that Christ is the one mediator and saviour of all (CCC 846; 1 Timothy 2:5). She also respects what is true and holy in other religions (Nostra Aetate 2), and teaches that those who, through no fault of their own, do not know Christ but seek God sincerely may be saved by his grace, which always comes through Christ (CCC 847).
rite: For the Syro-Malabar Church this is a family feast. The Thomas Christians have always called their way of life the Law of Thomas (Mar Thoma Margam), and the ancient churches the tradition attributes to him are still places of pilgrimage. Ephesians 2:20 is our own story: our Church stands “upon the foundation of the apostles”, and of one apostle in particular, who doubted, asked, believed and confessed “My Lord and my God”. The East Syriac tradition in which our faith was handed on came to us through the Church of the East, which also looked to Thomas as its father. On the same day, the Presentation of Mary invites families to offer their children to God, as Joachim and Anne offered theirs according to tradition.
study: Moses felt he was a “poor speaker”. What weakness do I offer as an excuse when God asks me to witness to him?
Isaiah says three times “Do not fear”. What fear is holding back my faith today?
St Thomas asked an honest question. What question would I like to bring to Jesus in prayer?
How can my family keep alive the faith that came to us from the apostle Thomas and pass it on to the next generation?
